jobs.description: No matter which side of the table youâve sat during interviews, youâve probably heard this question: âWhy do you want this new job?â In the recent past, Iâve interviewed a few candidates and heard the following answers so far: Iâm not learning much on the current job after itâs been 2-4 years. Iâm looking for something that offers better work-life balance. Iâm not really looking for a job. The recruiters got in touch and I thought Iâd discuss. Iâm looking for more challenging work. All of the above are valid answers. I think thereâs another perfectly valid answer that candidates seldom mention probably due to the gravity of the interview room situation. Iâve interviewed over a hundred candidates across different companies and am yet to find anyone that mentions: I am not happy with my current salary and benefits compared to my skills Back to topic of answers. So, when someone answers that they are not learning new things on the job, obviously, youâd be curios to know why and how they have tried to change things. Unfortunately, most candidates simply mention that they are doing repeat work and thereâs not much to learn doing the same thing over and over again. This is where I start feeling a little uneasy. However, I understand that itâs a true statement. If youâre in a similar situation, hereâs some suggestion: read books, and write code based on what youâve read. Then, you can tell a much convincing story that, Iâve forced myself to learn new things and hereâs some proof, but I really want to apply the newly learned skills outside the scope of the âhello worldâ skills. About work-life balance, I totally hear you. And if your current job doesnât suit what you need out of your life, itâs a perfectly valid reason to look for new opportunities. However, make sure youâre able to clearly set the expectation with your potential employer about what work-life balance means for you. For example, if you canât work over 40 hours a week, or must work from home one-two days a week, itâs best to discuss this even before an interview starts to ensure youâre a good match with the employer. If you showed up at in interview just because a recruiter got in touch, Iâd say introspect first. Itâs possible that on our subconcious mind you have expectations that the potential of the new job offers you something that you donât get at the current job. About looking for more challenge, it sounds like a cliche unless you can share examples of work that is of challenging to you. Creating and maintaining integration documentation including technical specifications, workflow and processes diagrams, implementation guides, and SOPs. Performing data QA and validation activities, including executing scripts and manual checks for data format, completeness, and accuracy. WHAT YOU'LL NEED FOR SUCCESS Bachelor’s degree in quantitative or technical field such as Computer Science, Health Informatics, Information Systems, Statistics, or equivalent experience. 3+ years of experience in a technical implementation, data integration, or data analytics in the healthcare industry. Working knowledge of healthcare data formats and standards (e.g., HL7, FHIR, CCDA, XML, JSON) Familiarity with clinical vocabularies and coding systems (e.g., CPT, ICD-10, SNOMED, NPI, RXNORM). Extensive experience working with data and technical integration projects that includes ETL pipeline, data normalization/processing, SFTP, and API connections Proficiency with cross-team project tracking/documentation tools such as Jira and Confluence Experience with data QA and validation processes. Familiarity in SQL, Python, and Bash for data querying and script execution Proven experience in leading technical implementation projects in healthcare, including client or vendor onboarding. Familiarity with cloud platforms such as AWS (S3, Lambda, Step Functions), GCP, or Azure. Understanding of healthcare workflows (e.g., care management, risk adjustment, quality improvement, revenue cycle, prior authorizations, value-based care). Strong communication and presentation skills for interfacing with clinical and technical stakeholders. WHAT WE'D LOVE FOR

jobs.description: *Dutch speaking* Wil jij jouw ervaring in klantcontact inzetten voor dossiers waarin niet altijd direct duidelijk is wie er aansprakelijk is? Als Klantenservice Medewerker Aansprakelijkheidsverzekeringen bij KCD behandel je uiteenlopende en soms complexe situaties. Je onderzoekt wat er precies is gebeurd, duikt in polisvoorwaarden en wet- en regelgeving en maakt vervolgens zelfstandig een goed onderbouwde beslissing. Geen standaard antwoorden, maar dossiers waarin jouw beoordelingsvermogen en aanpak écht het verschil maken. Je krijgt de verantwoordelijkheid om situaties van A tot Z te behandelen en hebt daarbij oog voor zowel de inhoud als de impact op de klant. De rol Als Klantenservice Medewerker Aansprakelijkheidsverzekeringen behandel je klantvragen en dossiers waarbij aansprakelijkheid niet altijd direct duidelijk is. Je brengt de situatie zorgvuldig in kaart, verzamelt de benodigde informatie en beoordeelt op basis van de feiten, polisvoorwaarden en geldende wet- en regelgeving wat de juiste afhandeling is. Je krijgt bijvoorbeeld een klant aan de lijn die als vriendendienst de badkamer bij zijn buurman betegelt, maar daarbij per ongeluk het nieuwe bad beschadigt. jobs.description: Headquarters: Mexico URL: http://lawnstarter.com About LawnStarter LawnStarter is the nation's leading on-demand marketplace for lawn care and related services, with over $150M in annual bookings. We're expanding beyond lawn care to become the one-stop shop for all home services. About Engineering Quality at LawnStarter Our QA team is growing, and we're investing real money in better test coverage. We already have shared quality standards and a QA squad that organizes itself horizontally across teams. What we don't have is someone dedicated to owning that vision: every QA is heads-down on their own team, so nobody has the room to drive the standards forward, unify how the squad works, or push the state of the art. That's the gap this role fills. It's not a nice-to-have we're adding because things are going well. It's the structure and leadership we need to make what we've already built actually compound. The Role You'll be LawnStarter's first Principal Quality Engineer, reporting directly to the Head of Engineering. We already have quality standards, working CI/CD gates, and AI tooling in the mix. Nobody owns the vision behind all of it, drives it forward, or leads the QA squad that keeps it running. You will. This isn't a QA management job today. You won't spend your day approving tickets or chasing bug counts. You'll take ownership of the standards and tooling that already exist, work collaboratively with the QA squad to improve them, and keep pushing the state of quality engineering forward as the org grows. As the QA squad grows, this role could take on direct people management of QAs, so hiring, coaching, and performance management experience is a real plus even though it's not the day-one job. You're not starting from zero, and you're not inheriting a mess either. That means the job isn't "invent a strategy nobody has thought about." It's "listen to the QAs who live in this every day, understand where the pain is, and lead them toward what's next." We need someone who reads where LawnStarter is today and builds from there, not someone who shows up with a favorite tool stack and a coverage number they picked before they met the team. What makes this role different: You own and evolve the quality strategy together with the QA team, instead of building one in a vacuum or just executing someone else's. You have direct sponsorship from the Head of Engineering and the room to keep growing the AI-native tooling already in the mix. Your success is measured by how much better the whole engineering org's quality gets under your leadership, not by a headcount number. What You'll Own Strategy and vision : The company-wide quality engineering roadmap, plus a quality accountability framework that spells out what engineers, EMs, and PMs each own at every stage of building software.
